marks: Bamboo slips buried in a tomb here around 300 BCE preserve the oldest known passages of the Daodejing.
By tradition Zhang Daoling received a revelation from the deified Laozi here in 142 and founded the Way of the Celestial Masters.
The Northern Wei emperor Taiwu received Daoist registers here in 442, making Daoism the religion of his state.
Laozi's traditional birthplace, where the Tang emperor Gaozong honoured him as an emperor in 666.

notes: The Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, and the Zhuangzi teach the Dao, the Way of nature, and acting through non-action; bamboo slips at Guodian (around 300 BCE) hold the oldest known passages.
Han rulers practise the teaching of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi; masters seek long life and immortality.
Zhang Daoling founds the Way of the Celestial Masters in Sichuan (142); the Yellow Turban rebellion of the Way of Great Peace shakes the Han (184).
Zhang Lu's Daoist state in Hanzhong submits to Cao Cao (215), and the Celestial Masters spread across northern China.
The Shangqing ("Highest Clarity") revelations at Maoshan (364–370) and the Lingbao scriptures enrich Daoist practice in the south.
The Northern Wei emperor Taiwu makes Daoism the religion of his state (442); Lu Xiujing catalogues the first Daoist canon (471).
The Tang emperors claim Laozi as their ancestor and honour him as an emperor (666); Daoist priests are sent to Korea (624).
Emperor Xuanzong orders every household to keep a copy of the Daodejing (733), which becomes an examination subject.
The Song court compiles a new Daoist canon; Mount Longhu becomes the seat of the Celestial Masters.
Wang Chongyang founds the monastic school of Complete Perfection (Quanzhen, 1167); Emperor Huizong (1100–1126) styles himself a Daoist sovereign.
The Quanzhen master Qiu Chuji meets Genghis Khan (1222); Quanzhen grows under Mongol favour, until Buddhist debates turn the court against it (1281).
The Ming court completes the printing of the Daoist Canon (1445); Wudang's temples are rebuilt on a grand scale.
Daoist priests serve temples, festivals and funerals across China and in Taiwan, while the Qing court favours Buddhism.
The 63rd Celestial Master moves to Taiwan (1949); Daoism is suppressed in China's Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) and revived since the 1980s.
Daoist priests and monastics serve temples in China, Taiwan and Chinese communities abroad, and its practices reach many millions more.
src: Isabelle Robinet, Taoism: Growth of a Religion (1997)
